label: Optimal Transport: Old and New
notes: Open by placing the whole book on one slide. Villani's introduction spans only four printed pages, yet it announces a subject that bridges probability, analysis, geometry, and dynamics. Tell students that today we build the map, not the proofs, so the later thirty chapters have a place to land.

label: Monge's Problem
notes: Stress the physical origin: Monge in 1781 asked how to move a pile of earth into an embankment with least total work. The unknown is a map sending each grain to a destination while preserving mass. Emphasize that the constraint, not just the cost, is what makes the problem hard.

label: Why Monge Is Hard
notes: Make the difficulty concrete. A deterministic map cannot split mass, so it may simply fail to exist when a single source atom must feed several targets. Point out that the cost is highly nonlinear in the map and the admissible set is awkward, which stalled the problem for over a century.

label: Kantorovich's Relaxation
notes: Introduce the decisive idea: replace maps by transport plans, that is couplings of the two measures. Now mass may split, the feasible set is convex, and a minimizer always exists under mild conditions. Note that every Monge map induces a plan, so Kantorovich genuinely enlarges Monge.

label: The Cost Functional
notes: Write the objective explicitly and read it aloud. The total cost integrates the local cost against the plan, and the quadratic cost is the one that links transport to geometry. Mention that the choice of cost determines everything downstream, from the structure of optimal maps to the metric that appears later.

label: Kantorovich Duality
notes: Present duality as the workhorse of the theory. Maximizing prices over the c-conjugacy constraint matches the minimum transport cost. The optimal potentials are the Kantorovich potentials, and their gradient will reconstruct the optimal map. Tell students that almost every existence proof in the book passes through this duality.

label: The Old: Structure of Optimal Maps
notes: Summarize the classical achievements. Under quadratic cost the optimal plan concentrates on the graph of a map that is the gradient of a convex function, Brenier's theorem. Cyclical monotonicity is the geometric fingerprint of optimality. These results, with regularity and the Monge problem, form Part One of the book.

label: Wasserstein Distance
notes: Define the metric that makes transport geometric. The square root of the optimal quadratic cost is the Wasserstein distance, turning the space of probability measures into a metric space. Emphasize that this is the object that lets us speak of geodesics, curvature, and gradient flows among distributions.

label: Displacement Interpolation
notes: Explain that Wasserstein geodesics move mass along straight particle paths, McCann's displacement interpolation. This dynamic picture is the hinge between old and new: convexity of entropy along these geodesics encodes Ricci curvature. Tell students this is where transport stops being a logistics problem and becomes differential geometry.

label: The New: Curvature and Gradient Flows
notes: Lay out the modern arc. Displacement convexity of entropy is equivalent to lower Ricci bounds, the Lott-Sturm-Villani synthetic definition. The heat equation is the gradient flow of entropy in Wasserstein space, Otto calculus. Functional inequalities then follow as convexity statements. This is the heart of the book's novelty.

label: Roadmap of the Three Parts
notes: Close with the structure of the journey. Part One develops the qualitative theory of transport; Part Two marries transport to Riemannian geometry through curvature and Otto calculus; Part Three pushes to synthetic Ricci bounds on metric measure spaces. Leave students with the single arc from Monge's earth to curvature.
